query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single-phase compositionally complex high-entropy alloy (e.g., equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi), dislocation motion under intermediate-temperature, high-strain-rate deformation induces rapid non-equilibrium nanosegregation of embrittling principal elements (specifically Ni, Cr, and Mn) at grain boundaries, thereby reducing local interfacial cohesion and transitioning the deformation mode from transgranular ductile to intergranular brittle fracture.
generation.material_initial_state: An initially homogenized, single-phase equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy with uniform elemental distribution.
generation.intervention: Subjecting samples to controlled uniaxial tensile deformation under two sets of conditions: (a) intermediate temperatures (e.g., 500–700°C) combined with relatively high strain rates to promote dislocation accumulation, and (b) higher temperatures (or lower strain rates) designed to allow for more uniform elemental diffusion.
generation.conditions: Deformation tests at two regimes: one at ~600°C with high strain rate (e.g., >10^-3 s^-1) and another at a higher temperature (~750°C) or lower strain rate (<10^-4 s^-1), within service-relevant conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation (or suppression) of nanoscale clusters enriched in embrittling elements (Ni, Cr, Mn) at the grain boundaries, as measured by atom probe tomography.
generation.mechanism: Under high strain rate at intermediate temperature, dislocation motion creates localized high energy sites that drive rapid, non-equilibrium diffusion of principal elements to the grain boundaries. This nanosegregation lowers the cohesive strength along the boundaries, triggering intergranular cracking and brittle fracture. In contrast, at higher temperatures or lower strain rates, enhanced diffusional homogenization prevents such localized concentration peaks, preserving ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples deformed under high-strain-rate intermediate-temperature conditions will exhibit clear grain-boundary nanosegregation (as detected by APT), reduced grain-boundary cohesion, and a shift toward intergranular brittle fracture (visible via in situ TEM and post-mortem fractography), with an estimated decrease in ductility (e.g., >30% reduction in elongation relative to baseline). Samples deformed under the alternative regime will maintain a more uniform elemental distribution and exhibit predominantly transgranular ductile fracture.
generation.baseline: The single-phase HEA deformed at conditions that do not promote segregation (e.g., higher temperature/lower strain rate) where uniform elemental distribution at grain boundaries is maintained and ductile transgranular fracture dominates.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies specifically to service and loading conditions where deformation-induced diffusion is significant (intermediate temperatures and high strain rates) and may not hold under quasi-static or very high-temperature conditions where diffusion equilibrates the elemental distribution.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative thresholds of strain rate and temperature necessary to trigger measurable nanosegregation, and the extent to which these effects may be influenced by additional factors like grain size, pre-existing defects, or minor alloying additions not altering the overall single-phase structure.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare several batches of the equiatomic CrMnFeCoNi HEA with identical microstructures. Deform specimens under the two defined regimes (high vs. lower tendency for segregation) while performing in situ TEM and subsequent APT mapping of grain boundaries. Simultaneously measure mechanical properties (tensile ductility, fracture mode) using high-resolution testing setups. Include control samples deformed at ambient conditions where nanosegregation is negligible.
measurements: Atom probe tomography to quantify elemental distribution at grain boundaries.
In situ TEM to observe dislocation dynamics and crack initiation.
Tensile stress-strain curves to assess ductility and fracture mode.
Fractographic analysis (SEM) to identify intergranular versus transgranular fracture.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If specimens deformed under high-strain-rate, intermediate-temperature conditions do not exhibit statistically significant grain-boundary enrichment of Ni, Cr, and Mn (relative to controls), or if the fracture mode remains transgranular and ductile (with ductility within ±10% of the baseline), then the hypothesis that dislocation-induced nanosegregation is the primary cause of brittle behavior in these HEAs would be refuted.

cited_evidence.text: Severe plastic deformation (SPD) is an effective approach to induce component element grain boundary segregation []. Both dislocations and defects generated during the deformation supply a driving force for the segregation behavior of solute atoms. The SPD techniques, such as surface mechanical grinding treatment and high-pressure torsion, have been successfully applied for Al and Mg alloys to obtain the grain boundary segregation structure and corresponding expected properties [,]. Notably, these methods are based on a considerable plasticity and acceptable deformation resistance at room temperature. However, for the ultrafine-grained RHEAs, the exceedingly high strength and limited ductility have brought considerable challenges to the SPD process. An increase in deformation temperature and reduction in strain rate are useful to improve the deformation performance. A higher temperature and lower strain rate are also conducive to a more adequate diffusion of solute atoms. Hence, based on the hot deformation technique and admissible plasticity of MoNbTaTiV RHEAs, the interaction between dislocation movement and multi-principal elemental atoms was used to obtain the grain boundary se

Ultrafine-grained MoNbTaTiV RHEAs were obtained via MA, spark plasma sintering, and hot deformation at various high temperatures and strain rates. With grain refinement and lattice strain increase, the large and inhomogeneous milled powder became refined and homogeneous after the MA. The component elements were segregated under relatively low temperatures and high strain rates. The fluctuation of element concentration occurred only near grain boundaries. The segregation gradually disappeared with the increase in deformation temperature and decrease in strain rate. The interaction between multi-principal elements and dislocation movement was responsible for component element segregation and determined the microhardness variations.

This study uncovers fundamental but latent mechanical mechanisms in MPEAs, advancing understanding of ultra‐strong bioinspired alloys.Keywords: bionic materials, microstructure design, multi‐principal element alloys, phase boundaries stability, strain distribution Strain localization along phase or grain boundaries leads to crack initiation typical of alloys. In multi‐principal element alloys, the enamel‐like microstructure is stabilized by phase boundaries. This facilitates trans‐phase migration of semi‐atomic surfaces and provides sufficient plastic space for dislocation‐mediated deformation. This approach overcomes the limitations of localized hardening of nanoscale microstructure alloys to mitigate strain localization.

During the tensile test process at intermediate temperatures in the air, intermetallic phases were not yet formed in coarse-grained Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni HEAs, owing to a short testing time (a few minutes). In addition, the above-mentioned oxide and hydrogen embrittlement mechanisms can be ruled out because these alloys show good resistance to oxidation at intermediate temperatures and hydrogen embrittlement at relatively low hydrogen concentrations (, ). These facts suggest that temperature-induced ductility loss in fcc-phase HEAs/MEAs could be related to segregation of some of the principal elements during the short testing time, which causes GB decohesion. We examined this hypothesis in an equiatomic Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA and revealed the fast segregation of Cr, Mn, and Ni separately into GBs, which accounts for ductility loss with increasing temperature. Correspondingly, we proposed and demonstrated that preexisting precipitates can migrate the fast segregation of Cr, Mn, and Ni into the precipitates instead of at GBs, which can effectively evade ductility loss during deformation at intermediate temperatures.

cited_evidence.kind: web:GB segregation engineering to enhance ductility
cited_evidence.text: Segregation of minor alloying elements to GBs often embrittles conventional alloys (, ). Grain refinement is an effective way to evade GB embrittlement because more interfaces reduce the level of individual GB segregation (). In contrast, multiple principal constitutive elements in HEAs can segregate into GBs instead of trace alloying elements. In HEAs, grain refinement can assist the segregation of principal constitutive elements to GBs and even lead to the formation of brittle intermetallic phases at GBs (). For example, Cr-rich bcc phases and L10-NiMn phases precipitate at GBs in nanocrystalline Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA (grain size, ~50 nm) after annealing at 450°C for only 5 min, which reduces the ductility substantially (). In addition, previous studies show that Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEAs with the grain sizes from 4.4 to 155 μm all exhibit loss of ductility at intermediate temperatures, irrespective of grain size in this range (Fig. 1). Microalloying with B in Fe-Mn steels has been reported to delay temper embrittlement at 450°C (). B can compete for GB sites and reduce GB energy and, thus, repel the embrittling element Mn due to the decreased driving force for Mn segregation

cited_evidence.text: Although the ductility of the dual-phase HEA is lower than the single-phase HEA at the testing temperature below 500°C, the ductility of the dual-phase HEA is greater than the single-phase HEA at 600° and 700°C. No intergranular embrittlement is observed. Figure 5 (B and C) shows the lateral surface in the vicinity of the fracture after tensile tests at 500° and 700°C, respectively. Figure 5 (D and E) exhibits typical ductile dimples on fracture surfaces after tensile tests at 500° and 700°C, respectively. In contrast to single-phase samples (Fig. 3D), the dual-phase sample has very few cracks near the lateral fracture surface. This suggests that the GB segregation engineering strategy via preexisting Cr-rich precipitates is effective to evade ductility loss at intermediate temperatures in HEAs. This is because the embrittling elements—such as Cr, Mn, or Ni—can be absorbed by preexisting embrittling element–enriched precipitates at GBs, which only leads to the growth of precipitates rather than GB embrittlement. However, when testing temperature was increased to 650°C, a significant hot ductility drop was observed for HT-1 sample. According to Figure 7(b), the facet cleavage surface and the limited amount of plastic deformation indicate that the failure mechanism was brittle intergranular fracture. The brittleness of HT-1 sample was even more pronounced under creep at 650°C as the creep fracture strain was only 0.03%. According to the local strain concentration at triple junctions of grain boundaries (Figure 11(a)), it is probable that HT-1 samples encountered an embrittlement at 650°C. papers.title: Grain boundary decohesion by nanoclustering Ni and Cr separately in CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys.
papers.approach: Used atom probe tomography and tensile testing at intermediate temperatures to trace nanosegregation of principal elements at grain boundaries; additionally, employed a GB segregation engineering strategy by introducing preexisting Cr-rich precipitates to redirect segregation.
papers.findings: Identified that nanoclustering of individual elements (Ni, Cr, and Mn) at grain boundaries correlates with ductility loss via intergranular cracking at intermediate temperatures; demonstrated that engineered dual-phase structures with Cr-rich σ phases absorb embrittling elements, improving ductility.
papers.mechanism: Fast nanosegregation of embrittling principal elements at grain boundaries reduces local cohesion and promotes crack initiation; directing these elements into preexisting secondary phases can mitigate brittle behavior.

papers.title: Deformation-induced grain boundary segregation in a powder-metallurgy ultrafine-grained MoNbTaTiV refractory high-entropy alloy.
papers.approach: Synthesized via mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering followed by hot deformation at varied temperatures and strain rates to analyze how processing conditions influence element segregation at GBs.
papers.findings: Observed that at lower deformation temperatures and higher strain rates, dislocation motion drives localized segregation of constituent elements to grain boundaries, which gradually diminishes with increasing temperature and slower deformation; segregation appears to modulate microhardness.
papers.mechanism: Dislocation-generated stress fields and enhanced diffusion due to stored lattice energy promote the accumulation of key elements at grain boundaries, potentially affecting toughness.

papers.title: Mitigating Strain Localization via Stabilized Phase Boundaries for Strengthening Multi-Principal Element Alloys.
papers.system: Multi-principal element alloys with enamel-inspired microstructure
papers.approach: Introduced nanoscale phase boundaries (comprising BCC and FCC phases) into MPEAs to emulate biological enamel microstructures; employed mechanical testing and atomic calculations to assess strain distribution.
papers.findings: Demonstrated that stabilized phase boundaries reduce strain localization, enabling trans-boundary dislocation transfer that results in excellent strength–ductility synergy without conventional heat treatment.
papers.mechanism: The phase boundaries serve as preferential sites for dislocation transfer, effectively delaying localized hardening and crack initiation; this mechanism contrasts with brittle intergranular fracture expected from conventional GB segregation.

papers.title: Effect of serrated grain boundary on tensile and creep properties of a precipitation strengthened high entropy alloy.
papers.system: Precipitation-strengthened high-entropy alloy processed by selective laser melting
papers.approach: Compared microstructures featuring straight versus serrated grain boundaries—with serration induced via controlled post heat-treatment—and conducted tensile and creep tests at 650°C complemented by molecular dynamics simulations.
papers.findings: Found that samples with serrated grain boundaries exhibited significantly improved high-temperature ductility (increased tensile fracture strain and creep rupture life) due to more homogeneous strain distribution and delayed intergranular crack propagation.
papers.mechanism: Serrated grain boundaries redistribute local strains and impede the formation and coalescence of intergranular cracks, contrasting with the embrittlement seen in alloys with straight GBs where segregation can lead to rapid failure.

established: Toughness degradation in conventional alloys is typically associated with grain-boundary segregation and the formation of brittle intergranular precipitates.

High-entropy alloys (HEAs) often exhibit favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening, yet they can still experience ductility loss linked to grain-boundary phenomena even in initially single‐phase microstructures.

approaches_tried.approach: Grain-boundary segregation engineering via preexisting Cr-rich precipitates
approaches_tried.outcome: Shifted segregation from GBs into secondary phases, effectively mitigating embrittlement and preserving ductility in CrMnFeCoNi HEAs.

approaches_tried.approach: Manipulating deformation conditions (temperature and strain rate) to control dislocation-induced segregation
approaches_tried.outcome: Demonstrated that high strain rates and low deformation temperatures enhance segregation, while higher temperatures and lower strain rates reduce it.

approaches_tried.approach: Engineering serrated grain boundaries through controlled cooling post heat treatment
approaches_tried.outcome: Produced grain boundaries with undulated morphology that distribute strain more evenly, reducing high-temperature brittle failure.

mechanisms: Dislocation-driven local diffusion leads to fast segregation of principal elements (such as Ni, Cr, and Mn) at grain boundaries, reducing interfacial cohesion.
Nanoclustering of embrittling elements at GBs initiates intergranular cracking.
Stabilized phase boundaries and serrated GB morphologies redistribute strain and defer the localization that triggers brittle fracture.
disagreements: The role of grain refinement versus increased interface area is debated – while grain refinement can promote uniform deformation, it may also enhance the extent of elemental segregation at GBs.

There is some divergence regarding the temperature dependency: some studies report that segregation diminishes at high temperatures in RHEAs due to slower dislocation motion, whereas conventional expectations suggest persistent GB embrittlement.
open_questions: What are the precise threshold conditions (in terms of temperature and strain rate) that govern the transition from ductile to brittle behavior in initially single-phase HEAs?
How do complex multi-principal element interactions influence the onset of grain-boundary segregation without the formation of intermetallics?
Can controlled experiments clearly distinguish between conventional segregation-induced embrittlement and the mechanisms unique to compositionally complex alloys?
opportunities: Designing controlled comparative tests between a baseline single-phase HEA and a variant incorporating engineered GB traps (e.g., preexisting precipitates) to directly assess segregation effects.
Utilizing in-situ TEM and atom-probe tomography under varying deformation conditions to map the evolution of dislocation structures and GB segregation in real time.

Exploring the synergy between controlled deformation parameters and micro-alloying to modulate GB segregation while retaining the single-phase, compositionally complex nature required for high-performance applications.

directions.direction: Systematically vary deformation conditions (temperature and strain rate) on a single‐phase HEA and use high‐resolution atom probe tomography (APT) plus in situ TEM to track in real time the evolution of grain‐boundary elemental nanosegregation.
directions.assessment: This approach directly targets whether dislocation‐induced segregation accumulates at grain boundaries under service‐relevant loading. It respects the constraint of keeping the alloy composition complex and single‐phase. Prior evidence from CrMnFeCoNi studies (e.g., PMC6897545 records) and the MoNbTaTiV HEA (PMC11407990 records) support the role of deformation-induced segregation. The experimental methods are well established and can yield quantitative thresholds for the transition from ductile to brittle behavior.

directions.direction: Introduce minor microalloying or engineered pre‐existing inert precipitates to act as sinks for potentially embrittling elements, thereby testing if redirecting segregation away from grain boundaries preserves toughness.
directions.assessment: This approach compares a baseline single‐phase HEA with a variant having engineered sites (such as Cr-rich precipitates) to absorb embrittling elements. It builds on strategies demonstrated in dual‐phase HEAs (PMC6897545 records) yet still retains a compositionally complex background. While the evidence supports GB segregation engineering, careful control is needed to ensure the alloy remains single‐phase or dual‐phase in a controlled manner.

directions.direction: Develop molecular dynamics and phase-field simulations that couple dislocation dynamics with diffusion kinetics to model the conditions under which nanosegregation occurs and triggers brittle intergranular failure.
directions.assessment: This computational approach leverages established physics and diffusion theories to predict critical strain rate and temperature thresholds. While it can directly probe the segregation mechanism and tie it to intergranular decohesion, its fidelity depends on parameters that must be validated experimentally, and such models are becoming mature but remain challenging in complex HEAs.

directions.direction: Perform systematic post-deformation annealing studies to assess whether relief of stored energy and rehomogenization reverses nanosegregation, thereby linking thermal history to toughness degradation.
directions.assessment: This method can distinguish whether observed brittle behavior is intrinsic to deformation-induced segregation or can be remedied by thermal treatments. There is supporting evidence from annealing studies in related HEAs (e.g., PMC9848264 and PMC11407990 records). However, the intervention must be finely controlled so as not to trigger unwanted phase transformations.

directions.direction: Conduct in situ high-temperature mechanical testing with simultaneous synchrotron X-ray diffraction to monitor both stress response and grain-boundary structural changes, comparing the onset of brittleness in HEAs versus conventional alloys.
directions.assessment: An in situ synchrotron-based approach under service-like, high-temperature conditions would directly observe microstructural transitions (e.g., nanosegregation, crack initiation) that lead to embrittlement. Although sophisticated, these experiments can clearly distinguish mechanisms in compositionally complex alloys from those in conventional alloys and are supported by prior work on GB behavior (e.g., PMC9848264 records).

choice.direction: Systematic variation of deformation conditions combined with high-resolution APT and in situ TEM to directly correlate dislocation-induced grain-boundary nanosegregation with the onset of brittle behavior in single-phase HEAs.
choice.why: This approach most directly targets the mechanistic hypothesis—namely, that under certain loading conditions (intermediate temperatures and high strain rates) the dislocation activity in compositionally complex HEAs drives rapid nanosegregation of principal elements (such as Ni, Cr, Mn) at grain boundaries, reducing local cohesion and leading to intergranular crack initiation. The combination of controlled mechanical testing and advanced characterization tools enables a clear, falsifiable comparison against the baseline uniform composition observed at lower strain rates or higher temperatures.
